1:1: This is an idiom meaning that the Lord spoke or communicated his message in some way.
1:2: Here, great means both large and important.
Get up is an idiom that means that Jonah should take action. It does not mean that he was sitting or lying down at the time that God spoke to him.
The pronoun it here, meaning the city of Nineveh, refers to the people living in and around the city.
Here, God speaks of evil as if it were something that has physically risen up in front of him as it has continually grown larger.
1:3: Here the words got up mean that Jonah took action in response to God’s command, but his action was to disobey instead of to obey.

The expression the face of the Lord represents his presence. The idea of the Lord’s presence also includes his knowledge, notice, attention, or judgment. By running away, Jonah is hoping that the Lord will not notice that he is disobeying. … “away from the Lord”
This city named Tarshish was in the direction opposite to Nineveh.
A ship is a a very large type of boat that can travel on the sea and carry many passengers or heavy cargo.
The author assumes that readers will know that fare refers to the price that a person pays to travel on a ship.
The ship is large enough that it has at least one lower deck that is inside the ship. This is where Jonah went.
1:4: Here, the author speaks of the ship as if it were a person who could think. This clause means that the storm was so severe that the ship was close to breaking apart.
1:5: The sailors were men who worked on a ship to control the sails and do other tasks.
The phrase a man to his god is an idiom meaning that each man cried out to his own god.
The author assumes that his audience will know that by his god he does not mean the true God, the Lord.
This could mean: (1) to make the ship lighter so that it would float better; or (2) to lighten or relieve a dangerous situation.
וְיוֹנָה יָרַד אֶל־יַרְכְּתֵי הַסְּפִינָה וַיִּשְׁכַּב וַיֵּרָדַם
This sentence provides background information about Jonah’s circumstances to help readers understand what happens next in the story.
1:6: וַיִּקְרַב אֵלָיו רַב הַחֹבֵל וַיֹּאמֶר לוֹ
The captain of the ship is the person who is in charge of the ship and the crew. The crew is another name for the group of sailors who work there.
The captain is using the question form to scold Jonah.
This is an idiom that communicates that the speaker objects to the behavior of the person being addressed.
While this phrase was used as an idiom in 1:2 and 1:3, meaning to prepare to begin the activity which was stated next, here the captain is telling Jonah literally to get up from sleeping.
To Cry out to someone means to loudly ask him for help.
אוּלַי יִתְעַשֵּׁת הָאֱלֹהִים לָנוּ וְלֹא נֹאבֵד
The implication is that Jonah’s god might not only notice them but save them.
1:7: The phrase a man to his friend is an idiom expressing reciprocal action. This means that the group together decided to do this.
Here, Come is an idiom that invites the hearer to begin an action with the speaker that the speaker names next.
We do not know the exact method that the sailors used to cast lots. It may have been with marked stones or pieces of wood. It was their method of getting a god to answer a question.
The phrase so that we may know implies that the men believed that the gods would control how the lots fell in order to tell them what they wanted to know. This was a form of divination.
The sailors are using the general term this evil to speak of the storm.
The expression the lot fell on Jonah is an idiom meaning that when the men cast lots, the result indicated Jonah. This does not mean that the lot literally fell down on top of Jonah.
1:8: הַגִּידָה־נָּא לָנוּ בַּאֲשֶׁר לְמִי־הָרָעָה הַזֹּאת לָנוּ
The sailors are asking Jonah to tell them who is responsible for the storm.
1:10: Here, feared a great fear is an emphatic construction that uses a verb and its object that both come from the same root.
The men on the ship used a rhetorical question to show how afraid and angry they were that Jonah was causing so much trouble for all of them.

This is an expression that refers to the face of the Lord to represent his presence. The idea of the Lord’s presence also includes his knowledge, notice, attention, or judgment. By running away, Jonah is hoping that the Lord will not notice that he is disobeying.
1:11: Here, going forward and storming is an idiom that means that the sea was becoming increasingly stormy.
1:13: They did not do as Jonah suggested. The implication is that the men did not want to throw Jonah into the sea.
1:14: These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words.
1:15: Here, the sea is spoken of as if it were a person who could rage.
1:16: Here, feared … {with} great fear is an emphatic construction that uses a verb and its object that both come from the same root. The danger of the storm is past; now they are in awe of the Lord’s power.
Here, both sacrificed a sacrifice and vowed vows use a verb and its object both that come from the same root to emphasize the ideas.
1:17: Some versions number this verse as the first verse of chapter 2.
2:2: This is poetic language. This line begins a poem describing Jonah’s experience in the fish, his prayer, and God’s answer. The poem describes these things from a time after they had already happened.
The implication is that the Lord answered Jonah’s prayer for help by helping him.
The two halves of this verse mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words.
Here Jonah is speaking of the fish’s belly as if it were Sheol, that is, the place of the dead. Jonah is expressing that he believed that this is where he would die very soon.

Sheol was the name of the place where they believed that people went after they died. It was thought to be a shadowy world located somewhere under the ground. The New Testament equivalent seems to be “Hades,” where the dead wait for judgment (see Rev. 20:13).
Here, you heard my voice is equivalent to the phrase “he answered me” in the previous line of poetry. In this context, Jonah is expressing that the Lord both heard him and acted to save him.
2:3: The terms the deep and the heart of the seas mean similar things. Jonah is using the two terms together for emphasis.
Here the term heart is a metaphor for the center of something. To be in the heart of the seas means to be completely surrounded by sea water.
The terms billows and waves mean similar things. Both of these are disturbances on the surface of the ocean. Jonah is using the two terms together for emphasis.
2:4: Here, eyes is a metonym meaning seeing, and seeing is a metonym for the knowledge, notice, and attention of God.
2:5: These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words.
Here the Hebrew term for life can also possibly mean “neck” or “breath” or “soul.” In any case, the water was threatening to end his life.
The word seaweed means a kind of long, stringy plant that grows in the sea.
2:6: Here Jonah is speaking of the earth under the water as if it had bars like a prison.

Here, the term pit has a double meaning. Jonah is in a deep place that could be called a pit, and this is also a word that is used in poetry for the place of the dead. Jonah is expressing that he felt certain that he would die in this place.
2:7: This phrase could mean that: (1) Jonah was already in the process of dying when he remembered the Lord; (2) Jonah had given up hope of being rescued and resigned himself to the fact that he would die.
The implication is that when Jonah remembered the Lord, he also prayed to him.
Jonah speaks as if his prayer could travel to God and his temple. This means that God heard his prayer and responded to it.
2:8: Here the term vanities of worthlessness is probably an idiom referring to idols of false gods.
Here, covenant faithfulness could refer to: (1) the faithfulness of God to his people; (2) the faithfulness of the people to God.
2:9: It is not clear whether Jonah planned to thank God by singing or shouting joyfully.
2:10: The content of what The Lord spoke was a command to vomit up Jonah.
3:1: This is an idiom meaning that the Lord spoke in some way.
3:2: Here, as in 1:2, great means both large and important.
וִּקְרָא אֵלֶיהָ אֶת־הַקְּרִיאָה אֲשֶׁר אָנֹכִי דֹּבֵר אֵלֶיךָ
Here, the pronoun it refers to the city of Nineveh, which represents the people who live there.
3:3: וַיָּקָם יוֹנָה וַיֵּלֶךְ אֶל־נִינְוֶה כִּדְבַר יְהוָה
Here the words got up mean that Jonah “took action” in response to God’s command to go as he did in 1:3, but this time he obeyed instead of disobeying.
Here, the word of the Lord represents the Lord himself.
וְנִינְוֵה הָיְתָה עִיר־גְּדוֹלָה לֵאלֹהִים מַהֲלַךְ שְׁלֹשֶׁת יָמִים
This sentence provides background information about the city of Nineveh to help readers understand what happens next in the story.
Here, because of the phrase a journey of three days, the focus of great seems to be the size of the city.
This could mean: (1) that a person had to walk for three days to completely go through the city from one side of the city to the opposite side; (2) that it took three days to see the whole city.
3:4: וַיָּחֶל יוֹנָה לָבוֹא בָעִיר מַהֲלַךְ יוֹם אֶחָד וַיִּקְרָא

The phrase a journey of one day could mean: (1) Jonah walked a day’s journey into the city and then he started calling out; (2) while Jonah was walking through the city on the first day, he started calling out.
3:5: Both fasting and wearing coarse cloth were symbolic actions that showed sadness or devotion to God or both.
3:6: The author assumes that his readers will understand that this word is Jonah’s message from God.

That the king rose up from his throne and he took off his robe shows that he was acting humbly. The throne and the royal robe were both symbols of his authority and power as king of a powerful nation.
A throne is a a special, ceremonial chair that a king sits on when performing his official duties as king. It is reserved for the king only.
The acts of putting on sackcloth and sitting on the ash heap are symbolic actions meant to show deep sorrow and repentance.
3:7: The implication is that the king sent messengers to make this proclamation.
The term nobles refers to important men who helped the king rule the city.
This refers to two groups of animals that people care for. A herd is made up of large livestock (such as oxen or cattle) and a flock is made up of small livestock (such as sheep or goats).
3:8: The implication is that these are the people’s domestic animals. They are not wild animals.
The writer assumes that his readers will understand what the people were to pray for.
Here, hands represents “doing.” This refers to the violence that the people of Nineveh were doing.
3:9: The king used this rhetorical question to get the people to think about something that is possible but uncertain: that if they would stop sinning, God might not kill them. It could be translated as a statement: “We do not know.” Or it could be stated as an initial word and be part of the next sentence: “Perhaps”
Here the author speaks of God changing his mind about bringing judgment as if God were turning around and walking in the opposite direction.
Here the burning of his nose is an idiom meaning that the person is angry.
3:10: Here the author is speaking of them stopping their sinning as if they turned away from walking on a path toward evil ways and started walking in the opposite direction.

The word translated as “evil” here is very broad, including moral evil, physical evil, and everything that is bad. It is the same word used in the previous sentence (and verse 8) to describe the actions of the Ninevites. The author is showing that when people repent of moral evil, God relents from doing physical evil (punishment). God never does moral evil.
4:1: Here, it made evil to Jonah a great evil is an emphatic construction that uses a verb and its object that both come from the same root.
The phrase it burned to him is an idiom that speaks of Jonah’s anger as if it were a fire burning inside him.
4:2: Jonah used this rhetorical question to tell God how angry he was.
The implication is that Jonah correctly foretold what would happen.
The phrase long of nostrils is an idiom meaning that the Lord does not get angry quickly.

Here, evil refers to the physical destruction of the city of Nineveh and its people. It does not refer to moral evil. In this context, this phrase means that God feels sadness about causing bad things to happen to people who sin, and he acts differently when sinners repent of their sin.
4:3: The implication is that Jonah wanted to die because God will not punish his former enemies.
4:4: The phrase it burns to you is an idiom that speaks of Jonah’s anger as if it were a fire burning inside him.
The reason for Jonah’s anger can be made explicit.
The Lord is using the question form to teach Jonah that he is not right to be angry.
4:5: The implication is that Jonah wanted to see whether God would destroy the city or not.
4:6: Here the term evil could be referring to one of two things (or both at the same time). It could be referring to: (1) Jonah’s physical discomfort or distress, meaning the intense heat of the sun shining on Jonah’s head. (2) Jonah’s wrong attitude concerning God’s decision not to destroy Nineveh. If both meanings can be preserved by using a general term, that is preferable.
Here, rejoiced with great rejoicing is an emphatic construction that uses a verb and its object that come from the same root.
4:7: The implication of it withered is that the plant became dry and died and would no longer shelter Jonah from the hot sun.
4:8: The implication is that a hot east wind will make Jonah very uncomfortable.
Here, the author speaks of the sun as if it were a person who could beat on another person.
The phrase on the head of Jonah may have a literal meaning or a figurative meaning. Perhaps Jonah felt the heat most on his head, or perhaps the phrase the head of Jonah means Jonah’s entire body.
4:9: God is using the question form to lead Jonah to draw a conclusion about his selfish attitude. God is not seeking information.
The phrases it burns to you and it burns to me are examples of an idiom that speaks of Jonah’s anger as if it were a fire burning inside him.
4:10: The expression son of describes a person or thing which shares the qualities of something else. This idiom, son of a night means that the plant existed only briefly.
4:11: God is using the question form to emphasize his claim that he should have compassion on Nineveh.

To make this verse simpler, it can be divided into two parts. The first part, ending with the great city, can be ended with a question mark. The rest of the verse can then be a statement, ending with a period.
